utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I'm glad to see that you are with us again, Mr. Mrksic. Mr. Borovic, we are ready to continue with your case; is that correct? Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Knowing what awaits us, that is Mr. Radic's testimony and we finally have Mr. Weiner with us in the courtroom, one thing I wanted to do before the start of Mr. Radic's testimony today was to discuss the proposal to have MFI 576 introduced. That is the one topic pending which requires Mr. Weiner's presence in the courtroom. So I thought it might be a good idea to discuss that first. My proposal is for Goran Hadzic's interview marked as MFI 576 be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Lukic, you're moving on. Mr. Borovic, does it trouble you if you are delayed a couple of minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my learned friend Mr. Borovic. I stand by my previous motion for the television interview given by Goran Hadzic, MFI 576, be admitted into evidence as well as the transcripts of that phone interview, marked as 3D00021, that's the television interview. The B/C/S transcript is 3D000214, and the English is marked as 3D000215. I would like to see whether anyone would still like to challenge that document before it is admitted into evidence, and I would like to add something to my motion. Last Friday I received a filing from the OTP regarding the possibility to admit certain Mrksic exhibits into evidence, that is dated the 6th of October. The text invoked by the OTP in paragraph 5 of that motion, and that is the reference to the Delalic ruling, I accept that and that is precisely why I believe that the relevance of this exhibit is now crystal clear. And I think there are no obstacles to having the MFI material admitted. I would, however, like to give Mr. Weiner a chance to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything from Mr. Domazet or Mr. Borovic? If not, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Your Honour, this is the second time that an attempt has been made to introduce this document through witnesses. The first time that the attempt was made was through Witness 002, which the Court will find on pages 10.636 through 10.638, and you can see the remarks of the Court in refusing to allow its admission. In that situation, that witness was asked about this interview. He had never seen it previously. He wasn't present for the interview. He wasn't able to discuss it and it didn't come in because -- due to an objection. Now, again, it was attempted to be introduced through a Defence witness called Dusan Jaksic, and the Court will notice it's on pages 11.962 through 11.964. Again, if we look at that we are in the exact same situation. Mr. Jaksic had never witnessed this interview, he had never seen it until he sat in this courtroom and it was played for him. He had no information about the contents of this interview. So there is no difference between the first situation, when it was refused admissibility, and this current situation. Now, as the Court knows videos in the past have been admissible before this Court; however, usually we have two types of videos, one are those depicting activity, depicting shelling, depicting a battle occurring, depicting a situation right after a battle so one can see the damage or can see what is happening during the battle. Or we've had interviews where persons are -- I'm sorry videos where persons are interviewed, where statements. And in both cases, whether it's the latter with interviews of a person or where it's observations of various activity, we have a witness who can describe it, who can tell you about it. Here we don't have that situation. We have an attempt by the Defence to introduce a statement, not through Rule 92 bis but however they want to introduce it through a video. They do not have the witness, they do not have so far any witness who can comment upon that. It's an attempt to introduce a statement of an alleged war criminal who is a fugitive. It's self-serving and it's not reliable. We would ask that it not be admitted at this time until they have a witness who can come here and tell us about this video, who can provide any reliability to it because at this time, there is no basis for reliability. I ask that their motion be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Mr. Lukic, is there anything in reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There has to be, Your Honour. Mr. Weiner's argument to the effect that this is a war criminal is something that the OTP knew when they placed this document in their 65 ter list and marked it as 336. It appears to clash with the present argument, but there is something else, too. There is an analogy in jurisprudence and there is one thing I would like to say. What I said the first time around when we talked about this interview and admitting it into evidence with P002, this was something that was tendered by the OTP in the Dokmanovic case when Mr. Goran Hadzic testified on the 25th of March, 1998. The transcript page is 3105 and that was in public session. I thought the OTP would be challenging this document with regard to the allegations in their motion, whether this sort of video footage is appropriate to be admitted into evidence at all. I thought it was the authenticity of the document that they were challenging. The first time around this was shown, not even the Trial Chamber had the transcript of this interview and now you are familiar with the transcript and the substance of that interview. There is one thing I'd like to say in argument, which I believe is sufficiently clear and which will support the admission of this exhibit into evidence regardless of whether there is a witness to corroborate this. We have the same sort of document in terms of date and substance by Mr. Borsinger to TV Belgrade on the 20th of November outside the hospital. I'm sure you will remember this was a TV interview that was tendered while Mr. Kiper was testifying on the 27th of March this year, and the transcript page is 6641. This was exhibited as 319. Mr. Kiper was never asked about the interview, not a word was said about it, and the interview appears to be identical to the present one, the same TV station, the same day, and it was exhibited with no obstacles whatsoever. The substance should be all right, unless the OTP mean to challenge the authenticity or the date of this interview, since they don't seem to be challenging the fact that the interview was given on the 20th of November. I do believe the interview to be a highly relevant one to the charges in the indictment and the facts therein. I also believe Mr. Borsinger's interview to be highly relevant to our case. Bearing in mind there is a transcript of Goran Hadzic's interview I wanted to avoid having it entered under Rule 92. The probative value of this interview in terms of whether he was a war criminal at the time or a witness and in which capacity he gave this interview or whether the OTP originally intended to exhibit this is only something that the Chamber can judge. In my closing argument, I will focus also on the reasons why the OTP are trying to challenge this document and oppose its admission. I believe that shows their true strategy. I do, however, believe that the Delalic ruling clearly tells us in this case why this exhibit is extremely relevant to our case, since it affects directly the allegations in our indictment. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Our decision is reserved. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Mr. -- just before Mr. Borovic starts, Mr. Theunens will be sitting in with us with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is leave, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it your client has been advised by you, Mr. Borovic, of his rights and his ability not to give evidence if he so wishes and that he need not answer questions which do not incriminate him. If your client would like to come to the witness position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before my client takes the stand, may I use this opportunity to say something before I start my examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may, Mr. Borovic. I would just point out that no doubt due to my error, page 6, line 414, there is a word "not incriminate." It should be "incriminate." We will give your client the affirmation now, Mr. Borovic. Would you read aloud the affirmation on the card?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before he does that, there is one problem that I would like to raise. The Defence has served on the OTP -- or rather, served on the OTP on the 2nd of October all the relevant materials that will be used throughout this testimony, the statements and the documents. Today, at 11.00, we received from the OTP an e-mail indicating the five documents that they would be using. This was at 11.00. I took two hours to go through the documents, and to discuss with my client what he would be shown and how he would comment on these documents. Not even a minute before we entered the courtroom I received a new e-mail from the OTP informing us that they would be using a further four documents. I believe this is a situation in which the Chamber should refuse the OTP the right to use these further documents since their notice was far too late. I had no time to confer with my client to see what the documents would be and in reference to just which circumstances. The first five documents are all right, the ones that were announced at 11.00, but the last four that I received came in too late. I think this is a bad strategy by the OTP, and I think this sort of strategy might impair our good relations that we have so far enjoyed throughout this trial. I think the Chamber should rule against this. Although this might in fact in no way impair the best interests of the Defence but it might be a violation of Article 21 of the Statute, a blatant one, in fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, of the four, one of them is a Defence exhibit which was tendered upon the Prosecution; it is the rules of infantry. The other are nothing more than statements of other persons to confront him with, basically the same as there has been testimony at the Belgrade court by a witness saying that you were in command of X unit. Those can be done with a document or those can be done without a document. We are not -- we were not looking -- we were not planning to put those documents to the witness other than just a statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it of those last three documents, people who gave that evidence in the Belgrade court are not to be called as witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That is correct. I'm just trying to think off-hand. I think one is Vujanovic, whose statement was also put to Mr. Jaksic. One is Kameni which is Milan Lancuzanin, and another one is the superior or the commander of this witness, which is Mr. Tesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, the Chamber will not receive in evidence those three documents, that is the transcripts of evidence or statements, whichever they are, of the last three witnesses you have mentioned. The -- nor will those documents be put to your client. But Mr. Weiner will be free to cross-examine without use of a document on the subject matter if he chooses. With respect to the fourth document, the first mentioned by Mr. Weiner, it's a standard official publication of the JNA at the time and I don't think that should be an issue, so that may be used. Thank you for that. Sorry to keep you. If you would now read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I hope the early stage-fright is now gone. Can you please share your personal details with the Trial Chamber? Can you tell them about your family? I'll try to avoid interrupting you frequently. We shall then be moving on to your career in the JNA from the very start to the time you left the JNA. Please go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. As everyone probably knows, my name is Miroslav Radic. I was born on the 10th of September in Zemun; it's a municipality belonging to Belgrade, to the greater Belgrade area. I completed my primary school in there. I went to the secondary military school in Belgrade and then completed two years at the military academy in Belgrade plus two further years of specialised training at the military school in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came to Belgrade, which positions did you first occupy in the army?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I completed the academy in July 1985. I was promoted to the rank second lieutenant and was sent to the Guards Motorised Brigade to serve as platoon commander, in one of the infantry battalions -- or rather, motorised battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After this you remained with the battalion or --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: After two years as platoon commander, I was appointed company commander within a special purpose battalion. A battalion securing buildings that we -- and facilities that were used for special purposes, including the memorial centre, the Josip Broz Tito Memorial Centre in Belgrade. I remained in that position for a full five years. After 1990, I became company commander in one of the infantry companies within the composition of the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Of which company were you a commander and for how long, until which year?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I started in mid-1990 and remained there until mid-1992, roughly speaking. This was the 3rd Company of the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: After this, I was appointed deputy commander of the military police battalion of the 46th Motorised Regiment. The regiment was stationed on a hill near Belgrade, the hill is known as Avala.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did you remain with the JNA for? And it might be a good idea to tell the Court right now what the reasons were behind you leaving the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I submitted a request to terminate my contract with the JNA on the 21st of June, 1993. The request was dealt with in October that same year. My reasons for leaving active service with the JNA were of a private nature. I explicitly stated this in my request.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radic, before we move on to Vukovar and what happened there, would you please be so kind as to tell the Trial Chamber about your family background? I did ask you about that, but I think you sort of skipped that in your first answer.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I'm married, father of two, and I have a son who is a student at the Belgrade university. My other son is still in secondary school. My wife is a judge at one of Belgrade's municipal courts and is currently serving as the deputy court president.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I think this should be sufficient for our purposes. I think we should now go on to describe how your unit arrived in the Vukovar area and when.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: The Guards Motorised Brigade on orders issued by the superior command was put in a state of combat alert on the 30th of September, 1991. The 1st Motorised Battalion within which my company was, set out in the early morning hours in marching order, in motor vehicles, in the following direction: Belgrade, Sid, Negoslavci. As we crossed over into the territory of the Republic of Croatia in the area of the village of Djelatovci, this marching column was fired at by the other side, using infantry weapons. So my unit was forced to stop so that the personnel would leave the motor vehicles. On that occasion, fortunately, none of the present soldiers or officers were wounded except for the materiel damage sustained by the motor vehicles, namely punctured tyres and shots at the vehicles themselves, no one was actually injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, and if so when, did you proceed along the charted course and when did you arrive at Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: That was the first situation that my unit was in a time of war, and it was only then that we realised how serious the task that we were given was. After a very short period of time, the unit proceeded, again in a marching order, towards the village of Negoslavci, but at one point in time again it had to stop because mortar fire was opened at the column. The superior command decided that all units from the 1st Motorised Battalion should continue, continue moving ahead on foot to a farm that was called Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How much time did you spend at Dubrava and did you work out any particular deployment in Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: As we arrived at the Dubrava farm, the marching column was met by the battalion commander himself, Major Borivoj Tesic, and he ordered me verbally the area and the direction in which my company was supposed to be deployed. I took up positions in that area and according to all combat rules, I deployed my soldiers and gave them assignments as to how they should be positioned in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us now when the unit started combat action and practically how it was brought into combat?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Before the unit started combat action, on the 1st of October of that year, in the evening hours, the commander of the battalion, Major Borivoj Tesic, called all the company commanders from within that battalion to come to a little house where the battalion's command post was, within the farm itself. That is where he issued a combat order to all companies individually, stating all the necessary elements for that combat order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion, did he tell you what you could come across while you're carrying out this task?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Within the combat order, Major Tesic told all the company commanders, including myself, that in Vukovar itself, we would come across a well-fortified and prepared enemy, consisting of paramilitary formations of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radic, could you please tell the Court whether at that time you were aware of the objective or the reason why the Guards Brigade came to Vukovar? Did you know?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: The objective why the Guards Brigade went to Vukovar was something that we were made aware of before we were actually sent to Vukovar. It was spelled out in specific terms through an order issued by the battalion commander at the command post, at the farm in Dubrava. At that moment, Major Tesic told us that the task of the Guards Brigade was to liberate the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army that was within the town itself, to lift in this way the blockade of the paramilitary forces of the Republic of Croatia, and also to free the non-Serb population that was in different basements, catacombs and shelters against their own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the command post, were you told anything else by Tesic in terms of these tasks, apart from the objectives you referred to just now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, was an explanation given to you as to where you were supposed to arrive, the direction in which you were supposed to act?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: That first evening, the battalion commander issued us an order in terms of what our tasks would be and how the unit would be brought into the region where we were expected to go, and from there the unit was supposed to launch an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you proceed, could you tell the Court what it means in military terms, this waiting sector, this region where this was expected to take place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: In military terms, a waiting sector is an area, piece of land, from where a unit is supposed to set out to launch an attack. That area is used for the last preparations to be carried out by the unit from a logistics and combat point of view, which is to say that the unit, prior to the attack, is being replenished with ammunition and other necessary resources used by officers and soldiers during an attack. In this waiting sector, the leaders of platoons - I'm talking about company level and rank - as well as squad leaders, receive their own combat tasks and they convey these tasks to their own subordinate soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was your waiting sector? How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of October just after midnight, that is to say in the early morning hours, while we were staying at the Dubrava farm, we were in a state of combat alert; and after a brief period of time, we rallied in a semi-open hangar. On the previous evening, the battalion commander told us that all companies would get guides who were local people from Vukovar itself, and whose task was to bring us safely to the Petrova Gora neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to the Court in a bit of detail what the neighbourhood of Petrova Gora in Vukovar is and where it actually is.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: The neighbourhood of Petrova Gora includes a part of the town of Vukovar which is to the west and southwest, and it includes the following streets -- or at least that was my understanding of Petrova Gora at the time: Namely, Ulica Oslobodjenje and Ulica Svetozara Markovica, the street of Svetozar Markovic from the very entrance into the town of Vukovar from the direction of the village of Negoslavci, and up to the area where there is an intersection of that street with Radnicka Street and also part of Radnicka Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript does not include the fact that he said it also includes the street of Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Am I right, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now explain what this first encounter looked like when you arrived in this waiting sector of Petrova Gora, how you felt, what you as a unit felt, and as a representative of the unit which was considered to be an elite unit, at least that is what the Prosecution claims.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Before I give an answer to your question, I would just like to ask for permission to give a brief introduction. On that night, the 2nd of October, when we left the Dubrava farm towards Vukovar itself, the most striking thing I recall to this day was the silence in which the unit or, rather, my company moved along during the night without any lights whatsoever. As for this silence, it was probably caused by fear, the fear that we soldiers and officers felt at the time. I can say quite freely, without any feeling of shame, that that fear was so great that it was almost palpable. We arrived in Petrova Gora in the early morning hours, around 5.00 in the morning, and full combat readiness was to be reached at 7.00. At Petrova Gora, we were met by individual local persons who I believed at the time were representatives of the territorial detachment that was at Petrova Gora. As for that detachment, the battalion commander, Mr. Tesic, said that they would act in concert together with us during the combat action. I wish to point out that I find this thesis a bit strange, namely the thesis that we had occasion to hear in this courtroom that the Guards Brigade was an elite unit in the Yugoslav People's Army, because I personally experienced and saw with my own eyes soldiers who were from my company, and I believe that this was the case with soldiers from other companies as well, who, during the course of the training that we carried out together with them in Belgrade, primarily carried out duties that had nothing whatsoever to do with combat training of persons or soldiers who are preparing for war action. For the most part, the duties we carried out were things related to protocol, like standing a guard of honour on special occasions and in special buildings. It is my understanding that an elite unit has to be trained and should be ready to carry out combat action, engage in combat action, in all kinds of terrain, in all situations that such a unit can find itself in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you then tell us specifically what it was that the Guards Motorised Brigade did. Where did you provide security and what did you actually do before you came to the area of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, I came to the Guards Brigade in 1985, and I was assigned to one of the two motorised battalions that had, as its task, to be involved in training for six months, that is to say training young soldiers, and then for six months to provide security for facilities, to stand a guard of honour at airports for visiting foreign dignitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please be so kind as to say whether you as a soldier heard of specialised units in western military forces or units that are called SAS, Alphas and Seals? First of all, have you heard of these units; and secondly, could you tell us whether you were that type of unit, that type of unit that was trained for action in built-up areas?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: According to the curriculum that was in place for various JNA units, there is a topic which deals with combat in settlements. However, it doesn't even come close to satisfy the needs in which we found ourselves, because apart from some technical points taught to soldiers during such a course, there is no mention of any psychological or other type of preparation of soldiers that could prepare them for situations they can encounter during an attack on a settlement. As officers, we try to teach them how to carry out an action against armoured vehicles and infantry in a settlement, but we do not prepare them psychologically. And in my view, that was one of the basic flaws of that type of training that we used to undergo. Special units, such as the ones you mentioned in various armies of economically powerful countries, undergo exclusively combat training, and they are being prepared for such combat situations specifically. On the other hand, JNA units prepare themselves for the most part for situations during combat but only to a very limited extent; this goes especially for the Guards Brigade because the soldiers there were specifically being prepared for the tasks I had mentioned, guards of honour, standing guard, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So as not to omit a topic which I believe is important, can you tell us what was the ethnic makeup of the Guards Motorised Brigade when you set off to Vukovar. Specifically in -- within the company you commanded, were there people of other ethnicities other than Serbs, that is?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: The guard unit was manned by A-class soldiers, and it was of mixed ethnic composition. This means that among its rank there were people from -- of various ethnicities, from all over former Yugoslavia, and this goes for soldiers as well as for officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There were assertions made here that once you were told to go to Vukovar, that members of the JNA who were of different ethnicity were basically prevented from going or even arrested so that they wouldn't go to the area of Vukovar. First of all, is that correct? And secondly, what was the ethnic composition of your unit?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: For the first question, that assertion is untrue. Those who were of Croatian ethnicity and who didn't want to be engaged in combat activities in Vukovar were given the chance or the opportunity to, based on their own decision, not to go to the area of Vukovar, and a smaller portion of those soldiers did not go in the first place. As regards the makeup of my unit, I recall that there were several Croatian soldiers there, and they left to the area of -- for the area of Vukovar together with the unit. Among them was my company courier, who was wounded after some ten days of action in Vukovar, and then he was returned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I know what his name is, but with all due respect for the Court, I don't want to create any problems for him, since this is a public hearing, and since he participated in the combat activities. Therefore, by your leave, I am willing to share his name with you provided we are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We will indeed occasionally go into private session, and that is perhaps when you will be able to give us that name. But my question is this: Within your unit and the Motorised Guards Brigade, there were Muslims, Hungarians, Montenegrins, Ruthenians, Macedonians, Albanians at the time of your arrival to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know about Albanians and Ruthenians, but the others were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now to go back to Petrova Gora. When you arrived in the area of Petrova Gora on the 2nd of October - and Petrova Gora was part of Vukovar, as you said - who did you meet there; and in brief, can you explain the functioning of the Territorial Defence in that area once you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: As I mentioned already, we arrived at Petrova Gora around 5.00 a.m. on the 2nd of October. Several local residents awaited us there, and it was my understanding that they were part of the local TO. That day I learned that this unit which was in the settlement of Petrova Gora was commanded by Miroljub Vujovic. I also learned that at Petrova Gora there was a command post of that detachment or, rather, of that unit, that there was also a rear command post, and both those posts were in a house of a gentleman. And I was told his last name was Antic and his rank was captain first class. I also learned that at Petrova Gora, there was a kitchen -- a cooking facility where food was being prepared for the local residents as well as the members of the TO Petrova Gora detachment. There was also a local outpatient clinic there, as well as a storage for ammunition and other materiel; this was a secondary storage, the principal one being at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As members of the JNA, and specifically as members of the 3rd Company, did you make use of their storage and their cooking facility and their rear services?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Occasionally we used their medical facility. As regards the other facilities, we didn't use them because at the battalion command level we had a rear platoon, the purpose of which was to supply all the companies with food, ammunition, and all other resources. And they were to draw that from the logistics base which was set up for all the units within the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that the members of the TO used their own facilities, their own storage, their own cooking facility and medical facilities; and you on the other hand had your own, apart from the medical facility you mentioned? And a question related to that is: Did you as the JNA have your own hospital in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: In Vukovar itself, there was no hospital. All those who had been wounded and were members of the JNA were transported to the village of Negoslavci, where the military hospital was set up, and this military hospital was part of the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you used separate facilities, the JNA on one hand and the TO on the other? Did you have your own different posts and facilities, including the medical facility, the kitchen, the ammo depot, fuel depot? Were all these facilities separate?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: As I've said already, we were supposed to have been supplied through our rear platoon. We were supposed to receive food, ammunition, fuel, and everything else we needed through them, and we were supposed to receive that from the battalion command. Company officers were tasked with taking those supplies at the place where the command platoon that was in charge of logistics within the 1st Battalion was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the Croatian paramilitary formations. They were one of your targets. My question is: Can you explain to the Chamber your first attack, provide some detail but not too much.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: The first attack commenced on the 2nd of October at 7.00 a.m. The unit set off from the settlement of Petrova Gora towards Nova Ulica, this being the direction of attack of my unit towards the river of Vuka. That attack --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: On that first day, the attack was characterised by the presence of fear among the young people who were all within the range of 18 to 20. It was understandable for me to see that. We were all together in the same boat and we were all well aware that we could lose our lives. All of my effort on that day and the days after that, for as long as we were in Vukovar, concentrated on trying to protect all those young people as best as I could, because I thought them children at the time and that they were sent there against their will - since they had to abide by the rule of law - and they were simply sucked into that conflict. It was clear to me that without specific help, those young people would not be able to perform all the combat actions required up to the end, without significant losses in manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was one of the immediate tasks of the company? What part of Vukovar, if you can recall, were you supposed to liberate on that first assignment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: My unit was given two combat tasks. The first one was received by myself at the Dubrava farm when Major Tesic, based on a map, issued orders to all company commanders, and he issued us with directions of attack. This included myself as well. I was tasked then to attack along the axis from the settlement of Petrova Gora via -- or rather, through Nova Ulica, through the settlement which at the time we called Leva Supoderica, all the way up to the road leaving Vukovar, leading to a neighbouring village. We were also to take the settlement of Seste Proleterske Divizije, which was south of river Vuka.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say Leva Supoderica, is that a part of a settlement or is it a street in that area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Leva Supoderica is a street connecting three other streets in the same neighbourhood. Because of a geographical feature known as Supoderica, these streets keep you from reaching the Bogdanovci road. However, in order to be able to get around more easily we referred to the whole neighbourhood as Leva Supoderica, although in actual fact I'm not sure that is its real name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness told us that there was such a neighbourhood as Desna Supoderica. Do you think that is a correct statement or is it in fact erroneous?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there is only one very short street called Desna Supoderica which is exactly across the way from Leva Supoderica and there is the Bogdanovac road passing between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was there such a unit as Desna Supoderica? Was there a unit known by that name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know. There was never a unit that was called that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry I interrupted you a minute ago. You were talking about that first mission. Can you tell us who was involved and how the enemy was operating, what weapons did they use against you and what was the outcome of that first mission?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Our first combat experience was peculiar in more ways than one. The battalion commander, Major Tesic, had told us that we would be supported by a local TO unit in this assignment; however, it wasn't ready for the attack on that first day, the unit which was supposed to be the unit adjacent to us. On that first day, my own unit was carrying out combat operations and some of our soldiers were wounded and injured as a result. On that first day, along the axis of operations of my unit, three tanks were damaged and put out of action; for me, that spelled a serious and considerable loss. At the junction of Nova and Bukajloviceva Streets, Bukajloviceva Street, at one point in time, one of the tanks that were added to the company was hit by a missile fired by the enemy. Soon after, it was hit several more times, so it caught fire eventually. There was nearly a full combat kit inside consisting of 40 anti-tank [as interpreted] mines. My concern at the time was that were those mines to explode, many soldiers would be wounded and killed among those standing near the tank. I decided to withdraw all the soldiers from that sector and to literally go back to our original position from which we had set out. That was our combat experience on that first day. I just wish to correct an error that I have noticed in the transcript. I said that there were 40 tank mines in that tank, not anti-tank mines, which means that this is a sort of mine which is used by these tanks to fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Radic. We could speed things along now a little, and if you could tell us how the Petrova Gora TO unit and the Leva Supoderica Detachment joined the fighting, as well as the volunteers arriving in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: The TO unit stationed at Petrova Gora joined the fighting the next day, as a neighbouring unit. The platoons from my company, based on the axis of operations that had been assigned them, worked together in the following way. On the one side, there were the JNA soldiers advancing, members of the Guards Brigade, and on the opposite side of the same street, you had the TO members advancing. I then noticed a problem, the problem being that the TO men were far better trained in the sense of having more combat experience, of being less scared. Soon the difference was obvious, in terms of experience and effectiveness, between the JNA men and the TO men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You talked about the command post of the 1st Motorised Battalion. Who manned the command post and what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Before I answer your question, I would just like to complete my previous answer. Along the axis of operations of my company there was a TO unit joining the next day. The volunteers arriving over the following period were being incorporated into the TO. As for the axis of operations of my company, on the 20th of October, a unit arrived that I was told was called the Leva Supoderica Detachment. And now for your question. Our battalion's command post was at Svetozara Markovica Street. It was at this command post that the command or the headquarters of the 1st Motorised Battalion or the 1st Assault Detachment was stationed. It was at the same command post that the commander of the TO staff was, Mr. Dusan Jaksic, who was then captain first class. Speaking of the command post itself, the battalion command -- or rather, the assault detachment, I wish to point out the following. The command post is a room and the command post implied also a handful of adjacent houses. The command itself was in one of those houses. In the command there were the battalion commander, Mr. Borivoje Tesic; his deputy, Captain Slavko Stijakovic; the general affairs officer, Mr. Bojic; and the battalion's signals officer, Sergeant Stamenkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At the start of combat operations, who were the TO men receiving their orders from and how did the combat plan evolve later on? Can you tell us more about this cooperation that you've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: The company commanders from our battalion received their assignments and reported on any assignments already carried out at the command post to the battalion commander himself on a daily basis. The TO commanders reported in that same place to Captain First Class Dusan Jaksic. Given the fact that Mr. Tesic and Mr. Jaksic were using the same rooms, it was only logical that they would be working on cooperation between the 1st Motorised Battalion and the TO detachment; the reason being, when the battalion commander, Major Tesic, issued assignments and missions to us specifying the axis of operations, he would always do this in the presence of Captain Jaksic. He would sometimes make suggestions whenever he deemed this to be necessary about the assignment in hand, based on which I concluded that those two were working closely together, while each of them issued assignments to their own subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Some time ago you told us that at the start of operations, the JNA were advancing down one side of the street, clearing the area, and the TO men were advancing down the opposite side of the street; and as a form of cooperation, this worked just fine. How many platoons did you have at the start of operations and who were they led by at the beginning, and what happened later on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: This form of cooperation might as well have gone on functioning well, but on the third day of operations what I believe was a tragedy occurred when the commander of my 1st Platoon, who was also my deputy, Lieutenant Vostic, Radoje Vostic, was killed. The very next day, the commander of the 3rd Platoon, Sergeant Dejan Jovanovic, was forced to leave the unit on health grounds. He had spine problems at the time, and the doctors who had examined him eventually advised him to leave the unit and not return. It was based on that that Major Tesic sent Sergeant Jovanovic to join a rear platoon. As a result, over the first four or five days, I was left without two platoon commanders. Given the fact that my company consisted of three platoons in addition to myself, the only one remaining was Second Lieutenant Elvir Hadzic, who had been trained at the high military academy but had completed a two-year course at the military school, simply because this was possible at the time. He had not done four years - that's what I'm trying to say - but only two instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Since we only have a little time left now, can you please tell us, if you remember this tragedy - that's how you define it - when your deputy was killed. Did someone manage to evacuate his body? What exactly happened, briefly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: This was the first tragedy that struck me in Vukovar and it was a truly painful one. On the 5th of October, when the platoon commanded by Lieutenant Vostic entered Osmog Marta Street, they came under mortar fire by the enemy. It was as a result of this mortar fire that he sustained a shrapnel wound to the head. They told me that he had been injured, and I came running to that place. I asked several soldiers to help me to crawl over to where he was because the first thing that occurred to me was that he had been wounded, or maybe he was just unconscious as a result of the explosion. However, when I finally reached his body, crawling on all fours, I realised that he had sustained a shrapnel wound to the head and that he was no longer alive. Regrettably, because of the exceptionally heavy mortar fire that we were under and because I did not wish to risk any further loss of life to the soldiers who were with me, I decided to leave his body behind in the place where he was killed. We weren't able to evacuate his body before the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this is a convenient time for our first break, so I'll have to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Ten past 4.00, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said that with your soldiers you got him out of that spot. A soldier says that he is the one who got him out, and he said that he carried out parts of his body actually in a blanket and that this afflicted him terribly and was therefore treated at the neuropsychiatric ward at the military medical hospital in Belgrade. Have you heard about that? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I'd like to correct you. I think I said that on that first day I tried to get him out together with a few soldiers, but because of the mortar fire we couldn't do that. On the following day, as for the body of the late Lieutenant Radoje Vostic, the members of the Territorial Defence got his body out in actual fact, those who had the courage to do that during the break, before the combat operations started on that day. They had the courage to go there -- that is to say at that time there was no combat. They had the courage to go there and to bring him back. I'm 100 per cent sure of that, and I know that not a single one of my soldiers took part in getting him out -- or rather, getting his mortal remains out. So that assertion is not true, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now be so kind as to tell us when it was that the Leva Supoderica Detachment came to your company's axis.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I remember certain dates. The first date was when Lieutenant Vostic got killed, and that was the 5th of October. On the 10th of October, one of my soldiers from my own company got killed; Djordje Nikolic was his name. At the moment when I was hit, fortunately it was only my pistol that got hit, the one that was on my belt, and I was taken to the hospital in Negoslavci. On the 18th of October -- or rather, I remember the 18th of October as the day when the only reservist got killed, the only reservist who was mobilised in Belgrade. He was mobilised and he joined my company. He was an ethnic Albanian. His name was Alija Gimani I think. I'm not sure. As for that date, when this reservist got killed -- or rather, two days after that date, the members of the Leva Supoderica Detachment came. So that was the 20th of October, therefore. And the battalion commander, Major Borivoj Tesic, introduced their commander to me, Milan Lancuzanin, nicknamed Kameni. And I was told that they would act in concert with my company and the Territorial Defence unit, that we would be engaged on the same task from that date onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he have his own command post, Milan Lancuzanin, or rather the Leva Supoderica Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Milan Lancuzanin was born in Vukovar, and his house was in the street called Leva Supoderica. His detachment probably got that same name on account of that street, and I know from various conversations with him that the original plan was for him to be deployed next to my right-hand neighbour, and that was the 2nd Company of our battalion that was commanded by Captain Zoran Zirojevic. However, he insisted with the battalion commander that he should come to where his house was. So it was on the basis of his own insistence that he was deployed there where my axis was. Since he was a local person from Vukovar who was familiar with the area, he himself chose his command post, which was in Nova Ulica, practically at the beginning of this street, viewed from the neighbourhood of Petrova Gora. In a house that belonged to a local person, his first name was Vasa, and his nickname was Robija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radic, you just mentioned your axis and the axis of operations. My question was whether an assault group was formed on your axis of operation and what can you tell us with regard to this important question?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Before I answer this question, I would like to make a brief introduction. Like the other company commanders, I was told that our battalion was -- on the basis of the first order of the brigade commander, Mr. Mile Mrksic, had the role of an assault unit, and it was the first assault unit within the Guards Brigade. The assault groups did not appear from the first day because the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment, Major Borivoj Tesic, did not issue an order for them to be established. After the first 20 or so days of carrying out our combat task, we, the company commanders, like the command of the 1st Assault Detachment, became aware of certain difficulties that we encountered during combat operations. I cannot remember exactly, but I know for sure that this was after the Leva Supoderica Detachment arrived. As far as I know, at the proposal of the commander of the Petrova Gora Territorial Defence detachment, and at the proposal of Miroljub Vujovic, who commanded a unit that was from Petrova Gora, the commander issued an order to establish an assault group along all the axes -- or rather, in all the companies. As for some more specific instructions, in terms of how this assault group was to be established, we did not have any. So after receiving this assignment, I consulted the company platoon rule, in which I read that an assault group should consist of a reinforced platoon with different kinds of equipment for combat support. Since the recommendation of the battalion commander, and therefore his order was that this assault group should be made up of the best soldiers, it was my understanding that this assault group would not involve my soldiers. At that time I thought, and I believe to this day, that from the point of view of combat, they were not capable of fighting the enemy in urban warfare, which is the most complex form of combat in built-up areas. Since that was the idea of Miroljub Vujovic, that assault group was established in a way so as to make it consist of the members of the Territorial Defence along my axis and of members of the Leva Supoderica Detachment. My role as company commander on that axis was to coordinate the assault group, the support group, which was also established at that point in time, and that was actually a platoon of 82-millimetre mortars, which came from the TO Petrova Gora and whose firing position was within Petrova Gora itself, the neighbourhood of Petrova Gora, that is, out in the open, together with soldiers that organised the security of the territory that this assault group was supposed to liberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you continue in greater detail about your tasks and about the combat itself, my specific question would be the following: Was the assault group a temporary formation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: As envisaged by the rules on the basis of which we carried out combat action, my company was a unit of establishment, and a company is a unit that does not change. It consists of soldiers belonging only to one of the services, and that is the infantry. In combat operations, it can be reinforced with different types of equipment, tanks, and other means of support, but only up to the strength of one platoon -- or rather, less than one platoon and up to one platoon. As for temporary formations that are established in order to carry out a particular task, they are assault groups; and in my axis an assault group was established, as I explained a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a temporary formation -- as it was a temporary formation, what did its actual strength depend on? Did it depend on the concrete task involved and did the strength, the number of personnel, change?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: That assault group that had been formed along the axis of the 3rd Assault Group, this being my axis as well, the axis I commanded over, was at the level of a squad. Its manning strength fluctuated, depending on the given task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Once a task is completed, what happens with a -- with the assault group? Members of that temporary formation, are they being returned to their home units once the task has been completed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I wanted to stress the following: In combat, the assault group was commanded by Miroslav Vujovic -- Miroljub Vujovic; I liaisoned between him and other elements of units which participated in that particular action that were at my axis. Every day, once actions were completed -- or rather, once there was no combat, all members of that assault group, so as to be able to continue functioning, would return to their home units, meaning if on that day there were four squads from among the members of the TO and each squad had around ten soldiers, they would then return to the TO unit and they would go home, according to Miroljub Vujovic's plans. As for the members of the Leva Supoderica Detachment, they had up to two or three squads within the assault group, and then they would return to their home unit, their home unit being the Leva Supoderica Detachment. They worked according to the plans of their commander, Milan Lancuzanin, a.k.a. Kameni.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This brings us to the time when you need to explain your role in detail as regards your tasks during combat. You started explaining that before, and could you please tell us: Once actions were completed for that day, what were you doing afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Since along the axis of operations of my company, I was the only officer who has completed the military academy, my task was to carry out coordination of all combat and non-combat elements of the units which were located along that particular axis. Those tasks included planning and the way combat operations were to be carried out. I also needed to plan the system of communication during combat, then the coordination between various elements of the assault group, as well as providing security and support - and the support, as I mentioned, was given by the mortar platoon. The tasks also included the use of medical facilities and various other rear services along my axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you would go into action the next day, there must have been some planning. What was that planning? Did you do it all by yourself or did you work on that with some other people? Could you please explain that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: If one wants to control and plan any combat activity, be it an attack or a defence, excuse me, one needs to do that thoroughly because the outcome of that operation depends on it. Since I mentioned a moment ago that I was the only officer who had completed the military academy, I didn't want to leave it to chance that anyone should plan combat operations except for myself. This means that Miroljub Vujovic didn't know how to do that. I also knew that Milan Lancuzanin couldn't do that. In order to protect the data and the system of communication, I did that exclusively. This means that each evening, after all daily activities had been completed, I withdrew to a separate room and I drew up the communications systems for each squad leader separately, using code names which usually included various colours, geographical terms and so on and so forth. This was done so that in the process of communication, no one but me could know who I was talking to and where that particular unit or part of the unit or squad is at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you used to distribute those plans to the squad commanders? At what time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Since I used to draw up such plans before any action, for the reasons of security, I would do that immediately prior to the -- prior to action. I never drew up a plan and set it aside for the next two days or so, but I would always do it the night before. Since we coordinated and since the battalion commander would tell us the exact time when we were to go into action at the level of battalion and the brigade, I always issued those orders to those commanders which were part of the assault group immediately prior to going into action, that is that morning. If we were to start attacking at 7.00 a.m. and if we all assembled at 6.30, I used to issue those tasks 10 to 15 minutes before we were supposed to set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've explained your role and how you coordinated, and we are now interested in hearing what the soldiers of your company were doing while you were busy coordinating.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: As I've said already, the system worked in a way that the assault group would begin its attack, and I was always with the assault group or immediately behind. This was done so that I could assist the implementation of the task and to be at hand to the commanders of squads from the motorised company, the 3rd Motorised Company, and I elevated the level of their responsibility once I was stripped of two of my platoon commanders, since Mr. Hadzic, Elvir, who was second lieutenant and the only officer along my axis. I didn't trust anyone else sufficiently, apart from him, to guide mortar fire by way of support for the assault group attacking. Therefore, that task of commanding, observing and guiding mortar fire - and the mortars we used were of 82-millimetre calibre - I gave that task to him. He was not the commander of that platoon of the 82-millimetre mortars but, rather, during combat he commanded that platoon since I knew that the soldiers from the TO were trained to use mortars, but I didn't know exactly to what extent they could command and guide mortar fire. And for purely security and safety reasons, I appointed him to command. The soldiers from the 3rd Company, during preparations the previous day, were issued tasks via their squad commanders as to which squad was to follow which part of the assault group depending on the streets that were supposed to be liberated that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I believe you said that the assault group which comprised members of the TO and volunteers, you said that that assault group went in front of your soldiers because they were more prepared and you tried to prevent any loss of life to your soldiers, I wanted to ask you what the tasks of your soldiers were then along that axis.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: As I said, they were 18, 19, 20, those young soldiers, and it was a heavy burden for them, imposed by the force of law. This is the way I saw things then, and I still think along the same lines. My efforts concentrated on trying to save or keep alive as many of them as possible, because at that time I saw them as my children. I behaved more like a parent than I would have had it been a peace situation in which we would have an ordinary officer/soldier relationship. These were no barracks conditions; these were conditions in which one could lose his or her life easily. On top of that, I kept repeating that I don't want them to bloody their hands, but, rather, to carry out a task of securing facilities which had been liberated and in that way to try and stay alive and not to be forced to face the enemy directly. And I constantly tried to prevent any of them having any contact with the enemy. Of course, I couldn't have all of them around me at all times so that I would know exactly what they were doing, but all of my effort was directed to that, to try and save as many of them. I was perfectly aware that it all depended on the way I carry out a particular task, and this could mean that they will survive or die.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since it seems we need to move along more quickly, you've explained your role, your coordination, so on and so forth, but I would like to know something else now. When there was no combat, where were you specifically? Say an action was completed, people were returned to their home units, and you've explained the role of the assault group. After all that, where would you go?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I have explained already the way it functioned in the field. After the completion of every action during October, that is until the 10th of November, members of the assault group would return to their home units. My soldiers were part of the security provided for the newly liberated territories. They were supposed to secure those areas. And I would tour all of them on a daily basis, and I would issue individual tasks to them. I also determined their direction of action and trying to warn them of the possible lines of attack by the enemy. I also provided instruction on securing facilities at night-time, and I tried to show them the tricks of the trade that I had learned at combat, as to how to secure a house and its approach. And often, I would spend the night with them in the same house because I knew they were afraid. I was hoping to show them that I was not, and I tried to convey my belief that they are capable of carrying out a task by merely being present there. Therefore, I lived the way they did. Once I had done all of this, as I've explained, and before the next day's fighting, I would withdraw and design the plans that I have spoken about. If no fighting was planned for the next day, sometimes I would stay with these soldiers and sleep in the same place as they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where was the place that you withdrew to? Where did you design these plans? What was this street called? Whose house was it? Can you please provide more detail.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: During this trial, we have heard evidence indicating that the house in which I was staying whenever I was resting was at Nova Street, Number 81. The house belonged to Stanko Vujanovic's father. It was in that house -- or rather, in the front yard of that house there was yet another smaller house with three rooms, two be used as bedrooms and one was used as a living-room. It was in this living-room that I would sit alone, write things down, jot things down, draw things up for the next day, in a bid to exercise my own command and control in such a way as to live up to the expectations placed by the task assigned to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you choose that house to stay in?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Stanko Vujanovic's father's house was a house built using solid materials; it had concrete foundations. I arrived at that house ten days after my original arrival in Vukovar. It wasn't on day one that I went straight to that house. At a briefing, the commander of the 1st Company, Captain Sasa Bojkovski, informed Major Tesic that he had been to that house at the exact time when it was hit by a missile fired by the paramilitary units. None of the people inside the house were harmed. Having heard that, I thought it was logical for me to go and have a look at the house. Having seen for myself that this was indeed true, and that the house was solid and safe, safe from mortar fire and other types of artillery fire, I decided to use that house as my observation post, of which I duly informed my battalion commander, Major Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you say "observation post," can you spell that out in purely military terms? What does that mean? What does that imply? Is that the place where a company commander normally stays?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Observation post is a combat element in the combat disposition of a company. If a company is on the defence, this observation post can be some sort of a large shelter. For example, it can be located on a clearing. During an attack, the observation post also has a role to play and is normally in the same place as the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now yes or no, please: What about Stanko Vujanovic's house -- or rather, his father's house at Nova Street 81, was it ever described as the main operations staff for the liberation of Vukovar, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was it ever described as the headquarters for the liberation of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was there ever a command post for the liberation of Vukovar in that house? Could it be used for that kind of purpose at all or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about the TO members and the Leva Supoderica men, did they ever come to your observation post at Nova Street 81; if so, why? Just as an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Of course they came. Normally they would come one by one. We have heard evidence here that meetings were held there, meetings of sorts. I myself was not the cabinet-type commander. I wasn't someone who would just receive his subordinate officers so that they could pay their respects. I was a commander who dealt with all problems and tasks as envisaged in the rules governing the work of company commanders. I would go and do commander reconnaissance wherever there was a problem. If there was a problem at Nova Street, that's where I would go. If there was a problem at Sava Kovacevic Street, that's where I would go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Were there any regular meetings held there, or could any one of those officers individually come to your observation post?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: No regular meetings were ever held in that house. I'll just give you one example that I remember. This was on the 20th when the Leva Supoderica Detachment arrived, and when Milan Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni, demanded to meet me. I told him to come. He brought six of his own commanders with him. We were in the small room in the small house because they all wanted to meet me. They all wanted to see who they would be working with, and that was their position. And this was the only meeting organised in this way and, for that purpose, that I ever held at that house; there was never another meeting. As for soldiers coming individually, soldiers who wanted, for one reason or the other, to talk to me and to seek my advice, is not something that I ever turned down. I wouldn't turn any of them away. Soldiers came to me for advice, and I dispensed advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for ease of following, can we please have a ground plan of Stanko Vujanovic's father's house on our Monitors, 2D11-0169.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And as soon as we have that brought up on our screens, please describe what you see. Is that the house you have in mind? Is that the house at Nova Street 81?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here "Nova Street 91." The number I see there is 91. This was added by the OTP when we forwarded this ground plan to them. It said "Nova Street," and they probably didn't know the house number. So somebody just put the figure 91 there. That's not our own entry, just for you to know, 91. At any rate, this is a document that we served in a timely manner on the OTP, and that's why we would like the witness to have a look and see whether this is consistent of the ground-plan of Stanko Vujanovic's father's house. Is this the house in which he had these talks and where he slept. I think this would be helpful to everyone because we haven't actually seen this ground-plan yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is this the house and is this Nova Street Number 81?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I want to say that I was the one who drew this ground-plan in 2004. I used this to explain to my own Defence team what this house was like, the house in which I was staying, meaning I was the one who drew this. I was the one who marked all these different things, with the exception of this number, 91. I really have no idea who added that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's of no consequence, but please tell us whether the ground-plan is consistent with the house at Nova Street 81.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is exactly the way I remember it to have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please describe what this means, this structure. Where were you? Where did you sleep and where was Stanko Vujanovic's father's family?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Since I'm familiar with the way things work in this courtroom, could I please have the magic pen so that I can mark things to make it easier for everyone to understanding what's going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that suggestion, Mr. Radic; you'll be receiving assistance immediately.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: If you look at the upper half of the page, you see Nova Street. That is the two words there. The house number is 81.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark that -- or rather change that over into 81.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: [Marks] So this number is not correct. On the left-hand side, marked by the number 1, is the gate for cars to enter the front yard of the house. Number 2 marks the door. On the right-hand side we can see the garage. I remember that throughout our time there, there was a pool-table inside which I marked as number 4. On the right-hand side of this sketch marked by the number 5 is a room, and that was used as a living-room. This is where I spent hours sitting, analysing, and planning before every operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please use a line to mark the direction from the door to the room marked as number 5. Where exactly would you have to go to get there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: You take the door first, then you go here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please put an arrow there.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please put a number 1 there, this path from the door to the room in which you worked.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that sometimes circumstances compelled me to work late into the night, it would sometimes happen that in the room that I marked as number 6, which was one of the bedrooms, I would spend the night right there. I didn't normally spend every night in that room. I didn't normally sleep there every night. I would normally sleep in the room marked as number 13, which is in the other house, the large house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please draw a line leading from number 13 to the place where you slept and put a number 2 there.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: The bed is on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please draw a line and put a number 2 there outside the sketch itself so we can follow.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: This is the place where I usually slept, not every night, but I never held a single meeting in this room, nor did I draw up any plans in this room, simply because there was sometimes quite a lot of people inside this house and I didn't want them to be privy to what I was doing. All my work was done in the room I marked as number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where is it Stanko Vujanovic's father was sleeping throughout this time that you spent at there house?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: When I first came to the house, which was sometime on or about the 10th of October, the only person staying in the house was Stanko Vujanovic's wife, Nada Kalaba. If you look at the ground floor, there is the number 10 right there which I used to mark the stairs leading up to the first floor. Throughout our time in the house, she slept in one of the rooms in the first floor. One thing I must say is I never even went up. I just didn't want to know what there was upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Then when was Stanko Vujanovic's father sleeping there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: It was just before the combat operations drew to a close. Stanko Vujanovic's father came to the house, and he would also sleep in a first floor room; I'm not sure which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Who else was sleeping in that house, the house that we described as the observation post?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: In this house the room that I marked as number 11 was a small kitchen with a dining area. To the left was the bathroom with a toilet. In this room that is marked number 13, I did not draw yet another bed which was right here, because I omitted to do that at the time. (redacted) (redacted), who was a sergeant in my company, slept on that bed; and every night when we went to bed, this table which is in the middle of the room is something that we moved to the side and on the floor next to these shelves, as I marked them, on blankets, on mattresses, on pillows, three soldiers from my company slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of -- what were the names of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: One of these three soldiers was Spasoje Petkovic; the second soldier was a Muslim, and his name was Suad Miljkovic; and the third soldier, I cannot remember his name right at this moment, but I know that it wasn't Elvir Masic. I know that it wasn't Dragan Vidacek. But right now I simply cannot remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to have this admitted into evidence, please, this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 783, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We've given quite a bit of our attention to this. We have to try to be as brief as possible. We need this sketch as part of our evidence because we heard some witnesses refer to these rooms and we can compare this description to the descriptions they gave. What about the members of the Territorial Defence and of the Leva Supoderica Detachment, where were they when there was no fighting? Where were they staying?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: The members of the TO of Petrova Gora were staying throughout the Petrova Gora neighbourhood. Every one of them stayed at their own homes, I think -- or rather, in the houses where those who moved into the Petrova Gora neighbourhood moved into because of the presence of the paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
