utterances.text: Sorry, the members of the Leva Supoderica Detachment were grouped around their command post, in several houses, so they were grouped in Nova Street, in a few houses around the command post where Milan Lancuzanin, nicknamed Kameni, was all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And where was this command post or the headquarters of Petrova Gora, and where was the Leva Supoderica headquarters at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: As we've heard so far, at the command post of the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment, there was the command post of the commander of the Territorial Defence Staff, Dusan Jaksic, captain first class, that is. As I've already said, the rear command post in Petrova Gora was in the house of Captain Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, is that a captain of the regular army or a reservist?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Captain Antic was a reserve officer who was within the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: And at that same command post, the rear command post, Miroljub Vujovic had his own post from which he took action and followed the orders that he had been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So that is the command post of the Petrova Gora Detachment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I never found out. I just know that at that place, this Captain Antic was rather at this place and once together with Miroljub Vujovic I went to this house; and together with them, I discussed certain matters and it was precisely at that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. As far as Leva Supoderica is concerned, you explained where their command post is. My specific question is as follows, and let us be very specific in the future. To the best of your knowledge, were Miroljub Vujovic, Milan Lancuzanin -- rather, did they go to see Major Tesic; and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I claim with responsibility that Milan Lancuzanin and Miroljub Vujovic did not come at the same time for briefings together with company commanders belonging to the 1st Battalion. I know that they, either in accordance with some plan of their own or at the invitation of Captain Jaksic or Major Tesic, they did go to that place because it was no secret that they were going there. But I know -- or at least that's the way I remember it, I do not remember either one of them being there together with us so that they could be issued the kind of orders that we were being issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. I think that's clear now. My next question is, and I hope that you will explain this briefly: Who came to your axis attack from the superior command? Do you remember any such thing? And if you do remember, tell us about it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that too. Major Borivoj Tesic, my battalion commander, came to see my unit up to the 10th of November on one occasion, and that was on the 2nd of November when we went together to the street of Vasilija Gacesa for command reconnaissance before the attack on the neighbourhood called Seste Proleterske Divizije.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about after that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: After that, Major Tesic, after Milovo Brdo fell - and that was on the 10th of November - was at Milovo Brdo every day, and he worked in accordance with his plan. And I was not aware of all the details, where he went and -- but practically every day I saw him at Milovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you know who General Adzic was at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I did know, most certainly. He was the chief of the General Staff of the then-Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did he ever come to the axis of your action, and did he ever visit the soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I did hear that he came, but I did not see him, and I did not have any knowledge about him being supposed to come. That is to say that at the moment when he was at my axis of action, I did not know that he was there, but later on, from Major Tesic, I heard that he was there together with Major Tesic and that Major Tesic showed him part of the territory where the 1st Motorised Battalion was staying and where it was conducting operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind that he knew -- that one knows one's soldier, is it possible that your soldier Elvir Masic could have been assigned to General Adzic's security detail when he came to visit Vukovar at that particular axis, and is that possible at all for someone from a platoon of your company to provide security for the chief of General Staff? Are you aware of any such thing, and could such a soldier have such an opportunity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: That is nonsense, and that is my most profound belief, because the chief of General Staff has his own personal security, consisting of professional officers so he did not require any supplementary security, particularly not from the soldier that you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to have a bit of water?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I'm fine. Everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your attitude was towards Major Sljivancanin at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin was the chief of security of the Guards Motorised Brigade. He was an officer from the superior command, and as such, I had an appropriate attitude towards him -- not only towards him but towards all officers who came from the superior command. After all, that is the attitude that I had towards my own commander, his deputy, and particularly towards all members of the staff of the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade. Major Sljivancanin came to my axis of action on several occasions, expressing his interest about the current situation that the unit was in, expressing his interest in the soldiers who were taken prisoner on the first day in the 1st Assault Detachment but not my axis, but he was looking for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to JNA soldiers? Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, JNA soldiers, yes. He was seeking information from us -- or rather, from me, as to what my knowledge was about the weapons that the other side had, possible prisoners, and I also have to note the following. On those occasions when he came to visit, he would always bring something to the soldiers. On one occasion, it was fruit juice, and several times it was cigarettes that were important, especially for those who were smokers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. What else can you say about him except for these few meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I can say -- I wish to say that I recall very well the moment when he came for the first time. That was when my unit was crossing the street of Otokar Kersovani. That was on the 21st of October, and when we were entering part of Cvetno Naselje. On that occasion, Major Sljivancanin came and brought a few packages of cans with fruit juice, and this fruit juice was distributed to all the soldiers in the area. The next time Major Sljivancanin came when the assault group liberated the neighbourhood of Seste Proleterske Divizije. I remember that that was on the 4th of November because on that day the Guards Brigade celebrated because that was marked as the day of the guards corps. The next time Major Sljivancanin came was when we entered the Bosko Buha neighbourhood, and I remember that it could have been the 8th or the 9th of November. We were together in a garage that was in the basement of a house, and from that garage Major Sljivancanin, through communications equipment, communicated with Jastreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Specifically, did he ever issue any orders to you? Did he issue any commands to you? Did he take part in any action planning together with you, or was that not the case?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: At that time, Major Sljivancanin, as an officer from the superior command, had the right to come to any unit, including my own, to seek information about the details that I talked about a few minutes ago. But I'm saying this with full responsibility, with the greatest responsibility, he never tried to interfere in the existing system of command and control, or did he ever issue me a single task or assignment, regardless of whether it had to do with combat or non-combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like Exhibit 156 to be placed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, it is a map on which I would like you to mark your participation in the combat depending on the time and place of combat, and we will go through this in detail so that we can compare that with various witness testimony. Is this sufficient or should we blow it up?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Could you please blow it up a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we also give a felt-tip pen to the witness so that he can mark various things on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you zoom in on the central part?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is it sufficient now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: A bit more, please. A bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is this sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Just so that I could be more precise, could you please zoom in some more?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I believe this will do.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Let us have the pen now. See what the times and place of action were, as regards your tasks.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I will mark off the basic elements so that it is clear to everyone where things are on the map. I will use the number 1 to mark the command post of the 1st Assault Detachment; it was in Svetozara Markovica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you say the number 1, are you trying to say that it actually marks the spot or can you place an arrow which points to the circle? No, the other way, the other way.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I marked it with a dot and a circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And then the arrow goes towards the number 1?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Nova Ulica as marked on the map is incorrect because I will point exactly where Nova Ulica is, and there is where the observation post was, where I was, this being the house with the number 81, Stanko Vujanovic's father's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you place the number 2 somewhere where the Danube is?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, very well. The street where this dot is is exactly Nova Ulica, Nova Street, whereas the street shown on this map is another street, Vrgoseva [phoen] Street. And immediately close by is Leva Supoderica, where Milan Lancuzanin, a.k.a. Kameni's, house was and I will mark that place with a number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: As regards the number 1, could you please erase the arrow next to it and put an arrow next to the dot indicating the exact spot? Put all the arrows there so that we avoid any confusion. The arrows should be pointing to the exact locations marked by numbers. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: For better visibility and so that it would be clear to everyone in the courtroom, could you give me another map, an unmarked one, where I could mark the direction of operations of my company and the times?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 784, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Borovic, this would be a good time for the break. We could resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Radic, with the assistance of the usher, who will yet again give you the pen, could you please mark on this Exhibit Number 156 the places of action and the directions, as we mentioned before the break?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: The area or the spot that I will mark with the number 1 is the staging area or the waiting sector from which my unit began with its combat operations. This is the neighbourhood of Petrova Gora, and I will mark it here with the number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put the arrow at the place where the staging area is?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, our unit was issued with two combat tasks. The first one was to start from the direction of the neighbourhood of Petrova Gora and along Nova Street and to carry out an attack along the axis of Petrova Naselje, then Leva Supoderica neighbourhood, and then the neighbourhood of Seste Proleterske Divizije in two stages. In the first stage, the attack commenced on the 2nd of October, and I will use this pen to mark off the right boundary, this being Nova Street. Therefore, on the 2nd of October of 1991, the attack commenced. In the first stage, my unit was to come as far as Bogdanovacki Put.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you just put the Roman numeral one there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, to state that this was stage 1. In stage 2, my unit was to liberate the neighbourhood of Seste Proleterske Divizije, which goes up to here, and I will put the Roman numeral 2 there. The first phase was completed on the 3rd of November. I will put the date here. And the second phase was completed on the 4th of November. That was our first combat assignment. The second one I received after having liberated the neighbourhood of Seste Proleterske Divizije, and the second task was also divided into two stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark that with stage 3, for clarification?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to add something. I wanted to put an arrow here in stage 1 so as to mark the direction of the attack of my company. In the next phase, our task was to carry out an attack along the axis of the neighbourhood of Seste Proleterske Divizije, the settlement of Bosko Buha, and the settlement of Milovo Brdo. In that third phase, so to say, we were to come as far as the Bosko Buha settlement. That was stage 3, and I'm putting the Roman numeral 3 here. The third phase was completed on or until the 9th of November. Milovo Brdo was taken - I will put the number 4 here - it was taken on the 10th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put an arrow and the number 2 where you've marked the third and the fourth phase of operations.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will do this the following way. I will mark this as the second assignment. Therefore, I put the number 2 here as the second assignment, and this is the assignment number 1. I will put it in a circle. I hope it is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Since you marked Petrova Gora with a number 1, would you then change that number into something else or maybe put the letter A so that we know this is Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I will try to erase this and I will mark it in a different way so that -- so that it is not a number. Therefore, we have the letter A for the neighbourhood of Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And you also changed the number 1 that you had put there previously?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If this is it, I would like to have this preserved and I would like to tender this as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 785, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, we have quite a graphic view of your direction of attack. My question is: What was the last time you coordinated the work of the assault group? What was the last time you coordinated its work?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: As I've said today already, the assault group, which was established along my axis, was temporary. At the moment the Milovo Brdo neighbourhood was liberated, I set about implementing my second combat assignment. After that day, I did not receive any task by the battalion commander, by anyone else - and here I have in mind his deputy in particular. I did not receive any other combat tasks which would involve coordination, command, or control of, be it regular or temporary formation, which means that on the 10th of November, I no longer commanded the assault group which was established along my axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you say "commanded," you mean coordinate, as you had described?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I've described how I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, you could have asked the witness to clarify whether he meant commanded, but you shouldn't have given him the other word.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was completely unintentional; but if I may correct myself, I will do the following way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you said "commanded" the assault group; what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I wanted to say this: My company, and I as the commander of the 3rd Company, were tasked with an axis of operations as part of the 1st Assault Detachment. As the most senior officer on that axis, I held both a moral obligation and an obligation as a human being to put to work all of my experience and knowledge in order to implement the task issued, while at the same time trying to save lives of as many people as possible. If I said I commanded the assault group, what I meant was that I coordinated the tasks of the assault group and the activities of the support units and the 3rd Motorised Brigade [as interpreted] as best I could and knew how, but all that stopped on the 10th of October [as interpreted] when I completed my second combat assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a mistake in the transcript. It says "the 3rd Motorised Brigade"; instead it should have been the "3rd Motorised Company."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. What did the members of the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Company do once the Milovo Brdo neighbourhood was liberated, and what were the tasks of the 1st Assault Detachment together with its commander, Borivoj Tesic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: We've had opportunity to hear a part of the story --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. There is something else that needs to be corrected in the transcript. It says that the assignment was carried out on the "10th of October," and it should be the "10th of November."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: During one of the briefings, when Milovo Brdo had been taken, the battalion commander, Borivoj Tesic, told us that all the Leva Supoderica TO members, as well as all the volunteers which were part of the two formations, were tasked with moving to another axis. The way I understood that, the other axis was the axis of the 2nd Assault Detachment, because they were not gaining any ground. Therefore, the Leva Supoderica TO members were to assist this second assault detachment in order for them to meet the goals of their combat assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know on what day Vukovar was liberated?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When was it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Vukovar was liberated on the 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Between the liberation of Milovo Brdo on the 10th of November and up until the 18th of November, 1991, your company was where and what were you doing during that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: During that time, the 3rd Motorised Company was in the area of the neighbourhood of Bosko Buha and Milovo Brdo. If you deem it important, I can mark off that area where my company was just so that it would be clear to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we have Exhibit 156 on the screen already, perhaps the accused, as a witness, could indicate where the second combat assignment ended.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What is the number 1?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: The number 1 is the neighbourhood of Bosko Buha. The number 2 is the neighbourhood of Milovo Brdo. The neighbourhoods of Bosko Buha and Milovo Brdo are actually two small neighbourhoods with a relatively small number of private homes. In that area the soldiers from my company, between the 10th of November and the 19th of November provided security of those homes in the two neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you put the number 3 next to the final position where the JNA units were once Vukovar was liberated, and this place should also include the volunteers and TO members. What was the final goal once Vukovar was liberated?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I put the number 2 next to the Milovo Brdo neighbourhood, and from that spot, in cooperation with the TO, various JNA units had to go as far as the Danube Hotel, and I will put the number 3 there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: As regards spots marked with numbers 1 and 2, between the 10th of November up until the liberation of Vukovar, were you engaged in any actions, did you carry out operations along an axis, or did you simply stay in this area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I've already said once that I completed my second combat assignment at the spot marked with the number 2, this being Milovo Brdo. After that, Major Borivoj Tesic, who commanded our battalion and our assault detachment and whom I could see daily at Milovo Brdo, took over command personally, and he personally controlled all actions and operations. This means that I was no longer engaged in any planning, commanding or controlling any unit between Milovo Brdo and the Danube Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this map as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 786, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the role and tasks of your company as of the moment you found out that combat or combat operations had ceased, and that was after the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: As I've said already, since my company was in the neighbourhoods of Bosko Buha and Milovo Brdo, on the 18th of November I was still with my company. I think it was sometime in the afternoon or in the early afternoon, when we learned by radio that Vukovar had finally been liberated and that the other side had surrendered. After that, by radio communication, the battalion commander ordered all company commanders to go from Negoslavci, where our vehicles were, to come to the town with all the trucks so that we could take care of all the people who were up until that moment in various shelters, basements, and so on and so forth, so that they could be transported from the centre of town, from the area where the bridges at River Vuka were, to Velepromet. In order to be able to assist the population, the commander of the anti-armour company, Captain Kopcic, Sladjan, was assigned that task. On that occasion, I was extremely surprised by the sheer number of people who came out of hiding and came to the area close to river Vuka and to the centre of town, around the Danube Hotel and Radnicki Dom. I never expected or presumed that there were so many people in Vukovar still; namely, when we received our combat assignments and tasks by our battalion commander, we were not told that there were so many people still in Vukovar. I thought that most of the population of Vukovar had left the town before the combat operations. As I said, I was very much surprised when I saw how many people there were after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you briefly. Throughout the combat operations, did you ever meet any civilians or were you always up against members of paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I can tell you with sure and certain knowledge that on that first mission between Petrova Gora and the Seste Proleterske Divizije neighbourhood, I never came across a single civilian. When we reached the Bosko Buha neighbourhood, I know that three persons were found who at the time were suspected of having fought with the enemy. These persons were sent to the battalion command as prisoners. I assume the battalion command then sent them off to Negoslavci. I don't know what became of them later, but I do know that this group of three included two senior citizens and one who was rather young. I think the group also included a lady. I never encountered any other civilians along any of my axes of operations, nor had I ever heard of any being in the area. The more I was surprised when I saw all the people coming out on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Where were you on the next day, the 19th of November, 1991, as far as you remember, and you have been reminded throughout this trial? Can you please tell us? It is, after all, a very important date for your position in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: On the morning of the 19th of November, I was with Second Lieutenant Hadzic and the other commanders from the 1st Battalion at Milovo Brdo. On that day, there were no combat operations and we all knew the war was over. I can't say specifically at what time, but it was around noon that Second Lieutenant Hadzic came to tell me that Major Tesic was asking to talk to me over a Motorola, over a radio. I called him back, and he ordered that I take a group of 20 soldiers and go to the hospital area which was about a kilometre away from the direction of Boso -- Borovo Naselje from the bridges over the river Vuka. I forwarded this order to -- Second Lieutenant Hadzic told him to gather the soldiers, after which we took several cars which had up to this point been used for both ferrying the wounded and injured, and drove over the bridge on the left-hand side as far as the hospital entrance. I can't remember the name of the street down which we drove to get there. We reached the hospital entrance, having entered the compound -- not the main gate, it was the auxiliary gate that we used and the street facing the gate is called Gunduliceva Street. It was virtually at the same time that we drove up to this entrance, and I was coming closer with my soldiers towards the back entrance that I saw Major Tesic approach from the opposite side; and he was accompanied by a lieutenant whom I didn't know at the time. They had several soldiers with them. We noticed each other arrive mutually and quite literally we met at the auxiliary entrance to the hospital, the one we used to describe throughout this trial as the emergency exit -- or rather, the emergency ward door.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you do anything with your soldiers in terms of securing the place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What exactly did you do? Where did you set up your security exactly in or around the hospital, and who did you see in the process?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: When Major Tesic and I met up at the auxiliary entrance to the hospital building, soon after, several minutes after, Captain Sasa Bojkovski arrived followed by several soldiers. In a way, because this was after all the first time we penetrated so deeply into an area that we had never trodden before, I was happy to see them all gathered in one spot. So in a way, I felt the safer for it. At this point, Major Tesic was standing at the hospital entrance, and he asked one of the hospital staff who appeared at the door to speak to Mrs. Vesna Bosanac. She soon turned up. Major Tesic introduced himself and said that he had been given the assignment of picking her up and going to the command post of the Guards Brigade so that the commander, Colonel Mrksic, could speak to her. As I knew at the time already what my own assignment was, at one point I turned to face Second Lieutenant Hadzic in order to carry out an assignment received previously from Major Tesic. At this point, Major Tesic and several other persons who were standing around him entered the hospital. I remained outside for several minutes to talk to Second Lieutenant Hadzic to see what the best way was to secure the hospital building. I told him that two soldiers should be placed at every entrance to the hospital to make sure that no one was able to access the hospital from outside and that no one would be allowed to leave without approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you enter the hospital at any point in time for any length of time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I did. Having imparted these brief instructions to Second Lieutenant Hadzic, I followed Major Tesic and Captain Bojkovski on their way in. I went to the basement where there were some rooms and a large crowd. To be quite honest, it was dark inside, so probably out of an abundance of caution I did not opt to go all the way in. But there was a room on the left in that corridor where I saw Major Tesic and Captain Bojkovski talking to someone. I approached them and realised that Sergeant Jovic was there, too, and we knew that he had been arrested the day the combat operations began.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you take Sergeant Jovic away from the hospital compound or did someone else do that? Did you personally take part in the taking away from the hospital compound of Sergeant Jovic and this other soldier, or was this done by someone else?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: In addition to Jovic, there were two other soldiers there, two reservists from our Guards Brigade. I did not personally take him away, but I did speak to Sergeant Jovic; and I spent several minutes in his company right there in that room, in which he was with those two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we need the 65 ter list now. I would like to show you some footage. The video is marked V000-0625-1-A, 1 hour, 16 minutes, 28 seconds, and then running all the way to 1 hour, 18 minutes, and 29 seconds. That is a very short portion, about two minutes long, and I don't think that should take up too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, can you see the video?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is in this video? Do you see a military uniform with a helmet there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: That's Major Borivoj Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: To his right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: A young man who he is caressing with his left hand so to speak. That's -- to my right, that's Sergeant Jovic. The civilian on the left is not someone I know. Standing behind them is a man with a pipe. And this is a Politika journalist; his name is Tomislav Peternek.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this Sergeant Jovic, the man in the middle?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's wearing a blue jacket. The person wearing a police uniform and a helmet on the left is not someone that I can actually identify. To Jovic's right is a person wearing a leather jacket and a green beret on his head. This is an officer from the same unit as Sergeant Jovic which is LSARD of the PVO. The name is Petar Devic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you perhaps notice that this person you just described has a sparse moustache, or do you think we should let the tape run on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Can we move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please replay the video briefly? There is one particular question that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Observe closely, please. Can you see yourself anywhere in this footage?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I think this is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So first of all my question was: This soldier wearing a green beret and a leather jacket taking Sergeant Jovic away, he was sporting a sparse moustache, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I did notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time see the soldiers being taken away from the hospital taken to ...

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: No, I am nowhere to be seen in this footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And were you actually there at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: When Sergeant Jovic was leaving, I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek that this footage be tendered into evidence, Your Honour. It had been shown before, but it wasn't tendered at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With Exhibit Number 787, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, having lingered briefly at the hospital on the 19th of November, what did you do next? Where did you go? And what became of the members of your unit, those who remained behind to secure the hospital, how long did they stay there for?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: At one point, Major Borivoj Tesic left with Mrs. Vesna Bosanac; I assume they went to Negoslavci. I stayed within the hospital compound, with Captain Sasa Bojkovski. The two of us walked around the hospital compound. Within minutes we each found two pistols that had been simply discarded. Based on the appearance of these pistols, since they weren't rusty or anything, there wasn't even dust on them, I inferred that the pistols had been discarded a short time before. Also, walking around the compound, near the gate that I took with the soldiers on my way in, there was a group of containers, beside which there were black bags or sacks containing different kinds of equipment previously used by the enemy, such as uniforms, military boots, military rucksacks, and so on and so forth. Soon after, several soldiers came to see me who had also found long-barrel weapons, meaning rifles, near the places where they stood guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the specific soldiers from your company who drew your attention to that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: No, their names escape me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. Having left the hospital compound, where did you go next? Did you first wait to see how long you would be expected to provide security for the external perimeter of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact time that Major Tesic returned to the compound. What I do know is he did come back at one point. As far as I remember, I had already left the hospital compound before he returned, leaving Second Lieutenant Hadzic to wait for the arrival of a military police unit commanded by Captain Paunovic as battalion commander -- or rather, one of the companies from his battalion, so that they would then take over from my company in terms of securing the hospital building. I know this all happened in a quick succession. I think it didn't take more than several hours, but I wasn't there for the actual handover and I wasn't physically present at the hospital at the time this occurred. One thing I do remember is I took the same way back that I had come. I went back to the area in which I had previously been staying, that means back to Nova Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you stop by to see anyone else from a different company on that day? Did you meet any soldiers or officers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I can't quite remember, but there is one thing I wish to say. After the liberation, that is on the 18th, since we were officers of the Guards Brigade, we all knew each other from our previous lives in the barracks. I thought it was the natural thing to do, to try and find out what had become of the rest of my friends and colleagues from the Guards Brigade. I remember meeting quite many of them in the downtown area, but I don't remember exactly when or who I spoke to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where Zoran Zirojevic was on the 19th of November, the commander of one of the companies within your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that together with me, Captain Sasa Bojkovski was at the hospital too. As far as I can remember, Captain Zoran Zirojevic was given a task by the battalion commander to clean up the mess at the Danube Hotel so that on the following day some press conference would be held at that hotel. I think that I stopped by then, but I cannot claim that that was on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where you were on the evening of the 19th, that is one day after the liberation of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 19th, in the evening, I remember that I got a new camouflage uniform, which at that time was not part of the regular equipment of infantry units; it was part of the equipment of military police units. I remember that on that evening, I was in the house where I had been staying beforehand too, that is to say Nova Number 81, and that I took a bath that evening, changed my uniform. And after a great deal of time, I gave myself the possibility to get a bit of rest, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to take you back to the 20th of November, 1991, that is to say the following day, that's a date that you heard several times here in court, can you remember where you were, what you were doing, where your company was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I wish to say that on the 19th, after the task of securing the hospital was accomplished, Lieutenant Hadzic carried out the handover of this security with one of the companies of the military police, which was commanded by Captain Milivoje Simic. During the course of that day --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the transcript did not include this part about the uniform. My colleague is telling me that the witness said that he got that uniform from an officer in his company. So the question is: From whom did you get that uniform on the evening of the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: On the evening of the 19th, I got the uniform from (redacted), an officer in my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: After returning to the area where I was staying before, too, I do not remember how this happened, possibly I was even at the battalion command too, or perhaps this was conveyed to me via radio communications, I was informed that the unit, after accomplishing its task, is to gather in a smaller area so that we would have control over the soldiers from the company in terms of discipline and in terms of security, because the question of security was accentuated by the battalion commander. So this was after the combat operations so that nothing would happen to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will continue, but I have a question. On that day, were you near the area where the hospital is, where the hospital compound is, and the like? So then when you finish your next question has to do with the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Since I talked about the period of the 19th, after the return from the hospital, I did not actually answer your previous question. What I'm trying to say is that as soon as the unit got back from the hospital compound, that is to say part of the unit, I issued an order to Hadzic to gather all the soldiers together in a small street that was parallel to Radnicka Street because I cannot remember what the name of that street is right now. But I know that all soldiers who had not been wounded and who had not left the unit for other reasons were concentrated in a few houses that were in the immediate vicinity of the house where I was. On the 20th of October --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: November.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, November. On the 20th of November, in the morning when I got up, together with Second Lieutenant Hadzic, I went to see these soldiers; and then after that, the two of us went to the centre of town. Before I go on telling you about what we did there, I wish to say that the soldiers from the entire battalion had the task of touring all the areas, all the axes of action where we had been staying, and where we were engaged in combat action, in order to collect all combat and non-combat equipment that we had been using and which had possibly been discarded for a variety of reasons. I personally issued that order to all squad leaders and their duty was to hand over this collected equipment to the company station, to (redacted), an officer within my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. And then you went with Hadzic to the centre of town, and then where did you proceed from there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: All of us felt the need to learn of certain information as to what was going on in different axes, who survived the war, who was wounded, what was going on further. We got this information through conversations with officers from the Guards Brigade. I remember that on that day, the 20th, Second Lieutenant Hadzic and I went to the centre and we stopped at the Danube Hotel; and then from the Danube Hotel, we went along a road that I knew, that is to say through the bridge on the left to the hospital. I had no idea what was going on in that hospital. At the moment when we arrived there, I saw a group of civilians who were moving towards the main gate. For the most part, these were women and children, and I was informed by those who were present that it was their own choice to leave, going either to Croatia or to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At that time, did you go into the hospital or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I claim with the greatest responsibility that I did not enter the hospital at all. I didn't take a single step there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And in the compound, did you come across any of your soldiers or commanders?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I claim with the greatest of responsibility that at that moment none of my soldiers were present, either in the hospital or in the compound around the hospital. I then saw many officers from the Guards Brigade. Among them I saw my commander, Major Tesic. As far as I can remember, I saw Colonel Pavkovic. As far as I can remember, I saw quite a few officers from the military police, but now I cannot give their names except for the names of the persons I've mentioned so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. How much time did you spend in the hospital compound, approximately that time; and where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: In the hospital compound, since I believed that something was going on there, something that I was not particularly interested in, I again took the same path towards the centre of town. And I want to say that at that moment, Second Lieutenant Hadzic and I went our separate ways because he stayed back talking to someone, whereas I set out towards the centre of town -- or rather, the Danube Hotel. I remember very well that as I was moving that way, towards the centre of town, at one point I noticed a group of people who were coming from the direction of the Vupik cellar. Allegedly, they had seen someone in that cellar. Out of sheer curiosity, I came to that cellar, and for the first time in my life I saw what a wine cellar looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, before you go on, I asked you something that is of interest to the Prosecution and especially to the Trial Chamber: How much time did you spend in the hospital compound? You didn't answer me.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I am sorry. I spent a very short period of time in the hospital compound. If I have to say how long it was, it was up to half an hour at the most. I believe it was even less.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. After the Vupik cellar, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: I would just wish to add something to that question of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: It was the first time I walked into that cellar and it was the first time that I saw the place where people were staying as they used that cellar as a shelter. In addition to these enormous barrels that were there of thousands of litres of wine that were in the central part of the cellar, on the left and on the right side, there were some make-shift things. I assume that civilians had been sleeping there, so there were mattresses there, blankets, and so on. I went through part of that cellar. But quite honestly, for safety and security reasons, I did not want to go throughout the cellar. I got out of it and from there I went to the Danube Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Two brief questions because we have to go, and we will complete your examination for today. On the 19th of November, were you at the briefing at the command post, with Borivoj Tesic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Like every evening, on that day too we had briefing with our commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did on the 20th of November, too; as I said, like every evening. In the period up to the combat actions and after that, the objective of these briefings was to inform the battalion command about what had been completed, in terms of the previously set tasks. On that 20th of November, at the battalion commander's command post, we were given the tasks that I had been talking about a few moments ago, that is to say we were given clearer instructions in terms of getting the soldiers together, getting materiel and technical equipment together. And we were also given the task of getting the soldiers back in shape so that they could look like proper soldiers, shaven, clean, because during the combat operations, we didn't have the right hygienic conditions. We could not get haircuts, shaves, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. So we have reached the 20th of November, the afternoon -- or rather, evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot deal with that in haste. I think that I will need about another half session. I did my best. I even made my witness hurry, but tomorrow I'm not going to take up more than half a session to complete my examination, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We adjourn now. We resume tomorrow morning at 9.30 and we sit tomorrow until 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 10th day of October, 2006, at 9.30 a.m. 25
